extracted.intended_audience: Researchers applying to the William T. Grant Foundation Research Grants on Reducing Inequality (2026)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for preparing letters of inquiry (and, if invited, full proposals) for the William T. Grant Foundation Research Grants on Reducing Inequality program. Covers eligibility, required materials, formatting, review criteria, and preferred project characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a specific inequality in youth outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must identify a specific inequality in youth outcomes. The program funds research to reduce inequality in academic, social, behavioral, or economic outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that outcomes are unequal in a brief discussion of existing literature; highlight the main explanations for the unequal outcomes that are relevant for your study. New for 2026: studies that primarily focus on physical health outcomes (e.g., physical illness, clinical trials) are not funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify dimension(s) of inequality to be addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a convincing case for the dimension(s) of inequality the study will address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funded dimensions: race, ethnicity, economic standing, sexual or gender minority status (e.g., LGBTQ+ youth), language minority status, or immigrant origin status. Specify the groups on which the study will focus (avoid vague terms such as 'at-risk youth,' 'disadvantaged youth,' or 'vulnerable youth'). Offer a well-developed conceptualization of inequality—avoid treating dimensions as mere variables; provide conceptual/theoretical insight into why and how the identified inequality exists. Research focusing on other dimensions must be in intersection with one of the prioritized dimensions; the Foundation will not primarily fund studies centered on other dimensions (e.g., disability) alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate theory of change and policy/practice relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Articulate how findings from your research will help build, test, or increase understanding of a program, policy, or practice to reduce the identified inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw on extant theoretical and empirical literature to provide a rationale for why the specific program/policy/practice will equalize outcomes or improve outcomes for a group. Specify your theory of change and identify how the study will investigate this rationale empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with Research Interests (alignment with program)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed study must align with the program’s research interests: it should examine a program, policy, or practice intended to reduce inequality in the specified outcomes and dimensions for youth ages 5–25 in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies focused primarily on documenting causes and consequences of inequality are not a fit. The letter must make clear how findings will inform implementable policies, practices, or programs; general statements about relevance to policy/practice are inadequate. Inequality can be reduced either by interventions that help some groups more or strategic application of universal approaches that disproportionately benefit those who need it most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualization and Relevance (theoretical mastery and contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of inquiry must reflect mastery of relevant theory and empirical findings and state the theoretical and empirical contributions the study will make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss how findings will be relevant to policy or practice and present a compelling theory of change or explanation for why the program/policy/practice is likely to reduce inequality in youth outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: rigorous and appropriate to goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed methods (quantitative, qualitative, or mixed) must be rigorous and commensurate with the project's goals, and design, methods, and analysis must align with the research questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description of research design should make clear how empirical work will test, refine, or elaborate theoretical notions. Quantitative analyses should emphasize hypotheses and plans for testing them; qualitative analyses should explain how they will illuminate processes. Mixed-methods proposals must clearly and compellingly describe integration plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and case selection appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Plans for case selection, sampling, and measurement must clearly state why they are well-suited to address the research questions or hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples must be appropriate in size and composition; qualitative case selection (critical, comparative, etc.) must be appropriate for the questions. For quantitative causal analyses, provide convincing evidence of adequate statistical power—particularly for subgroup analyses (e.g., differences between racial/ethnic groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis plan quality and awareness of limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantitative and/or qualitative analysis plan must demonstrate awareness of the strengths and limits of the analytic techniques and how they will be applied in the current case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, discuss potential generalizability of findings and show plans for validating measures. If using qualitative data, provide detail about coding processes and the plan for establishing coding reliability. If proposing to develop or improve measures, discuss how you will show measures are valid and reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility: realistic timeline, staffing, and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed methods, time frame, staffing plan, and other resources must be realistic and demonstrate that the project can be completed as proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assure that data will be successfully collected, describe the team’s prior experience collecting such data, and identify strategies to maximize response rates and access to data sources. Prior training and publications should demonstrate the team's track record. Clearly justify the unique value and specific role of each team member; avoid teams with many senior investigators listed for limited time without clear justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and length requirements for LOI and narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of inquiry must follow specified file and formatting constraints: the LOI functions as a five-page proposal; Project Narrative is five pages maximum with specified formatting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project Narrative format: 12-point Times New Roman, single-spaced text with a line space between paragraphs, numbered pages, 1-inch margins; reference list (if any) included in the upload will not count toward the five-page maximum. LOI includes project information fields (title, dates, total requested amount), and a brief description limited to 1,500 characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project brief (1,500 characters) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The short project description (1,500 characters) must concisely summarize the project for the online application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the major research questions or aims; briefly summarize the project’s rationale and background; describe the research methods, data analysis plan, and intervention (if applicable). Use language appropriate for an educated lay audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project Narrative content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The five-page Project Narrative must state questions/aims, provide a strong rationale, include hypotheses, and describe methods and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a brief literature review showing how the project complements existing theory and empirical research; describe theories and the theory of change; state relevance for policy/practice; provide specific hypotheses or research questions; detail sample/case description and selection procedures, research design, key constructs, data sources and collection procedures, and intervention (if applicable); summarize data analysis plan and identify key measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum vitae / biographical sketch requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a one-page curriculum vitae, biographical sketch, or resume for each Principal Investigator and Co-Principal Investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-page maximum; include education and training, peer-reviewed publications, and grants. Do not submit full CVs or multiple-page resumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers' research grants LOI additional materials and institutional requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers’ research grant letters of inquiry must include budget and organizational documents and require institutional sign-off prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must submit a full line-item budget and budget justification (templates provided); indirect costs may not exceed 15% of total direct costs; include the applicant organization’s IRS tax-exempt determination letter and the organization’s most recent audited financial statement. Institutional signature is required prior to submission—coordinate with your institution and allow time to secure sign-off. Officers’ research grants are awarded on the merit of the LOI alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect cost cap
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect costs requested may not exceed 15 percent of total direct costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This cap applies to both Major Research Grants and Officers’ Research Grants; include indirect costs within the total requested amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: organizational and study scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible applicants: tax-exempt organizations only; the Foundation does not make grants to individuals. Eligible studies must align with program interests and relate to outcomes for U.S. youth ages 5–25.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Foundation encourages proposals from under-represented institutions (HBCUs, HSIs, Tribal Colleges, Alaska Native-Serving, Native Hawaiian-Serving, AANAPISI). The Foundation defers to the applying organization’s criteria for who may serve as PI/Co-PI, but expects investigators to have experience and skills to carry out the work. Non-research activities (program implementation, operational costs, fundraising, endowments, general operating budgets, scholarships) are not supported; LOIs for ineligible projects are screened out without further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission limit per PI
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit only one application per cycle as the Principal Investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: you may submit only one major grant LOI or one Officers’ research award LOI in a cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disciplinary jargon; use lay audience language
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the LOI and summary materials in language appropriate for an educated lay audience because internal reviewers may lack deep knowledge of an applicant’s specific area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some LOIs will also be reviewed by youth reviewers in addition to staff; plain-language clarity is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study types supported and not supported
rubrics_metrics.description: The program funds descriptive studies that explain how programs/policies/practices reduce inequality and intervention studies that provide causal evidence on effectiveness; it does not fund studies focused primarily on causes/extent/consequences of inequality or those centered on physical health outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive studies should clarify mechanisms or explain how/why a program/policy/practice operates to reduce inequality. Intervention studies should provide causal evidence (e.g., randomized designs) on effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power for quantitative subgroup analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: If proposing quantitative analyses of a causal nature, demonstrate that the study will be adequately powered to detect effects, particularly for any subgroups of interest (e.g., differences between racial and ethnic groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide convincing evidence regarding sample size and power; for cluster randomized designs, consider applying for additional funding to ensure sufficient sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative reliability and measurement validity
rubrics_metrics.description: If using qualitative data, provide detail about coding processes and plans for establishing coding reliability; if proposing to develop or improve measures, discuss how you will show measures are valid and reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain procedures to ensure trustworthiness of qualitative inferences and psychometric properties of developed measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: mixed methods and interdisciplinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation values projects that harness the learning potential of mixed methods and interdisciplinary approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where appropriate, demonstrate how methods and disciplinary perspectives are integrated and how mixing methods advances understanding of mechanisms or causal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: meaningful practitioner/policymaker involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation values research that involves practitioners or policymakers in meaningful ways to shape research questions, interpret results, and communicate implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how practitioners/policymakers will be engaged at stages such as design, interpretation, and dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: mentorship and team composition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation values teams that combine senior and junior staff in ways that facilitate mentoring of junior staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about roles and mentorship structures; avoid token inclusion of junior investigators without substantive mentoring plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: leadership from underrepresented researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation seeks to support projects led by members of racial or ethnic groups underrepresented in academic fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight leadership and principal roles of investigators from underrepresented groups where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: data generation and sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects that generate data useful to other researchers and make such data available for public use are valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe plans for data documentation, archiving, and sharing consistent with ethical and legal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference: creativity and field advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Foundation values projects demonstrating significant creativity and potential to advance the field (e.g., introducing new paradigms or extending methods, measures, and analytic tools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe innovations in design, measurement, or analysis that enable stronger inference or comparability across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget sensitivity to study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget expectations vary by study design: secondary data analysis projects typically fall at the lower end of the budget range; new data collection and sample recruitment projects and experiments usually require larger budgets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major research grants: $100,000–$600,000 over 2–3 years; Officers’ research grants: $25,000–$50,000 over 1–2 years. Consider supplemental funding for resource-intensive designs (e.g., cluster randomized trials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application review process and timeline expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the review process and expected timelines for decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters of inquiry accepted early January and late July. For Officers’ research grants, funding decisions are emailed ~14 weeks after LOI. For major research grants, invitations to submit full proposals are emailed ~9 weeks after LOI; full proposal review to Board decision takes ~10–12 months from LOI. Full proposals (if invited) follow a ~25-page narrative format, require IRB approval before funds are issued, and are reviewed by 2+ external reviewers plus internal Senior Program Team and Board review. Applicants may be asked to respond to critiques before final funding recommendations.
